article.title: The Politics of Winning
article.author: Cleveland DSA
article.content: by Justin W. What does it mean to win? Why do you want to win? What are you willing to do to answer those two questions? For years, the Democratic Party has taken the position that “winning” is all that matters. As a Marxist, I argue that the reason Democrats run for office is to get into office; no more, no less. Power for the sake of power. At times we will see some platitudes, some rhetoric about making the world better, but we rarely see any movement on issues or legislation that will materially affect our lives. Nothing can be done because Democrats need to win the next election and can’t alienate anyone; but also no one else can take power to do anything because they won’t “win.” Since 2016 the Democratic Party has been the party of “No Trump” and, while trying to be a bulwark against the excessive cruelties of the Republican Party is nice, there is no goal beyond that. We know this because, when pressed on why we should vote for their candidates, the response is “do you want the Republicans to win?” There is always something better on the horizon and we must vote now to secure the chance for that future alternative. What is that alternative, you might ask? Who knows. Whatever you want it to be. So long as it’s not “unreasonable.” There is a hollowness at the heart of liberalism in America. In 1992 Francis Fukuyama wrote The End of History and the Last Man . In it, he claimed that we had reached “the end of history”, that liberalism had won out and there was no political change necessary beyond some tweaks to current policy. What we see from the Democratic Party is the end result of that belief. There is no future, only a (supposed) bulwark against those who want to drag us back to the past. A (supposed) protection from fascism. Amy Acton is the Democratic nominee running in Ohio’s gubernatorial election. She recently said, “I do not support boys playing in girls sports” amidst a wave of anti trans attacks made by the Trump administration alongside capitulation from organizations like the Cleveland Clinic that have trans people losing access to the healthcare they need. She, as the representative for the Democratic Party of Ohio, has made it clear to trans people that they are not worth protecting. This is considered a strategic move on her part by not just the Democratic Party, but by pundits and consultants as well. It is considered by many a “necessary” move to win the seat. That view, the one peddled by consultants and think tanks, is how we need to view not just Amy Acton’s actions, but those of the Democratic Party she is part of, especially given that the Democratic Party as an organization has funded anti-trans ads. The liberal view of power is one marked by distrust in individuals, not systems. “Power corrupts” is a classic example of the liberal view of positions of power doing the corruption, not the system rewarding the corruption. To a liberal mindset, corruption is an aberration, not an end result. It should be noted this is true for all liberal worldviews, neo-liberalism and progressive liberalism just the same. It is a view that nurtures the mentality that simply voting someone out of a seat will solve all the problems of the world with no other work needed. It then follows that winning elected office must always be the goal of every organization, every campaign, and every protest. Ultimately, the end goal is to vote in the correct person, and they will solve all the problems of the world for you. This has two effects. The first is that it allows a person to view only the outward symptoms of the problem. There need not be systemic analysis or deeper understanding of fixing problems if all that is needed to save the world is to switch out leadership. This allows for a very limited understanding of the world, mirroring the anti-intellectualism of American culture. Second, it means that once that person is in power you can “go back to brunch.” Given the lack of systemic analysis and the belief in the “Great Man” theory of change, voting in the correct person means that anyone holding this worldview needs to develop neither militancy or discipline. There doesn’t need to be a sacrifice of anyone’s time (other than voting) nor a dedication to learning (other than who to vote for) to weigh a person down. As said before, you can go back to brunch, and that is more appealing than many would like to admit. This stunted and naive view of power, because it is easier to grasp, is held by most in America, especially consultants. Elections must be won, there are no other alternatives to power. This view must be understood before we ask why Amy Acton decided to throw trans people to the proverbial curb. Given that elections are the only (to liberals) battleground for power, we must ask what is required to win. What you must be willing to do to be the bulwark against the horror of the other side winning. One might assume that certain principles can’t be sacrificed and some lines must be left uncrossed, but that isn’t true. How many lines we should be willing to cross is directly proportional to how “evil” the opposition is perceived to be. Previous, low stakes elections may have simple decorum tossed aside. Other elections might have some people taking money from unsavory corporations who aren’t on the “right side”. However, with the slide towards fascism and economic ruin constantly on the horizon, the stakes are high, and anyone and anything can be tossed aside for “the greater good”. Every argument of “well they have to say that to win elections” or “that’s what it takes to win an election” are built from the belief that you must win at all costs. Nothing can be left on the table. With a Marxist, systemic view of power in mind we rightly see this as the system rewarding corrupt behavior and politics that care for no one. Given the incentive structure, anyone with a systemic view of power can see that the person with the most “flexible” ethics will win more often. This is not the case for a liberal worldview. A liberal worldview does not view systems as evil nor rewarding to corruption. It does not view the sacrifices of principles, politics, nor posture as inhibiting or even untrustworthy. Merely functional. This is also why politicians receive such uncritical views of their politics, despite all evidence to the contrary. This is best seen in Donald Trump where some of his followers believe he will clear out “The Deep State” despite him clearly being in the Epstein files. Not to leave out the progressives, Alexandria Ocasio Cortez is believed to be against Israel and capitalism despite the funding she has given to the iron dome and staunch defense of “free markets.” I have even heard some people say Nancy Pelosi is for universal healthcare despite repeated declarations of opposition spanning more than the last decade. These cults of personality exist because any position taken on any subject can be seen as “campaign promises” or “necessary positioning” and not a reflection of true belief. This unscrupulous behavior works because everyone else is doing it. This is why those deemed to speak their “true beliefs” are admired so much, because it is a reprieve from the “business as usual” politicians, even when some of those people are obvious liars, like Donald Trump. We can ask ourselves if “Winning” works, but I do not believe that to be the correct question. The cracks have been forming for some time now and the fact that the Democratic Party lost to Donald Trump, one of the most hated politicians in US history, should make it clear that “Winning” is something that cannot happen forever. The DSA has received the influx we currently see because of the hatred generated by the callous incompetence of the Democratic Party. Instead we should ask why would someone choose to “Win” instead of doing good. Why getting into office must be the ONLY goal. Why Democrats always seek power for the sake of having power. Power corrupts, and therefore cannot be used. However, power must be held lest it fall into the hands of the unworthy. This contradiction explains both the reason Democrats will not act with the power they have but also why they must do whatever it takes to win. For Republicans, this flips to those deemed worthy shall use the power of office. It also explains why some politicians have the cults of personality they do. Both views are built from the same premise: whomever is “worthy” should wield that power as they see fit. How do we know who is “worthy”? By “Winning”, of course! Returning to Amy Acton and her throwing trans people to the proverbial curb, we now see more clearly why she is willing to sacrifice a certain subset of the population to “save” the rest. While Amy might not make it worse for trans people, she will also not help them. Power corrupts, after all. This makes her victory hollow. When we know there is nothing that will be done, what celebration can there be? It is merely a delay to the horrors the Republican Party might bring forth in the next election. The worst part is that we all know and accept that. We know there will only be a continuation of the demonization of trans and queer people, with the Democrats doing nothing. Democrats continue to make the decision to abandon parts of their base for the goal of keeping power out of unworthy hands, while saving no one with the power they obtain. I frequently wonder how aware the Democrats are of this. Through this, “Winning” becomes the only goal. “Winning” is the only position one can have. “Winning” is the only strategy, the only thing that matters. From all this we see a “Politics of Winning.” If you are to criticize Amy Acton, ask her not to throw trans people under the bus, you are giving up the race. If you ask Kamala not to bomb Palestine, you are hurting our chances to win. If you criticize any Democrat, in any way at all, you are criticizing victory itself. What will they do with elected office? Doesn’t matter. They’ve proven themselves worthy of power, therefore nothing they do can be wrong. As socialists, we should all reject the belief of corrupting power, but we also need to reject the “Politics of Winning” as well. We reject the idea that power corrupts, because we know that systems incentivize certain actions and behavior. Through a materialist lens we understand why certain behaviors are selected for and elevated over others. We understand that it is easier and simpler to be unprincipled in a system that rewards shortcuts and lies. Unscrupulous decisions, “campaign promises”, and strategic jettisoning of certain members of the population are rewarded, not punished under the current system. We can know and understand that this is a problem, but that does not make us immune to the trap of that mentality. We must hold our principles of democracy and accountability even closer, because we understand how easy it is to give in. We must act in good faith because we know how much bad faith is rewarded. We must build structures of organizing that do not replicate what has come before because we know what it incentivizes. We must believe in our fellow workers, our comrades, and in the future we can build together. There can be no shortcuts for us to take in building this new world. We must be more willing to lose with our principles than to win with our compromises. Say no to hollow victories, and the politics of winning.
